lead: Pressure tells how hard a fluid pushes on each unit of area. It is force per area acting perpendicular to a surface. In a static fluid, pressure rises steadily with depth because each layer carries the weight of fluid above it. This one idea sizes water tanks, dams, submarine hulls, pipeline test pressures and the reading on a tap gauge. Engineers use absolute pressure for gas laws, gauge pressure for instruments, and pressure head for pumps and pipes. This chapter builds those three views and the simple depth rule that connects them.
prereq: You need: density and specific weight from Ch 1.2; force and weight ideas from basic mechanics.

blocks.text: Pressure p is normal force F divided by area A: p = F/A. The force must be perpendicular to the surface; a tilted force contributes only its normal part. The unit is pascal, 1 Pa = 1 N/m². A kilopascal is 1000 Pa, and 1 bar is 100 kPa. Pressure at a point is a scalar: no direction. The force it produces is normal to the chosen surface.

blocks.where: p is pressure in Pa; F is normal force in N; A is area in m².

blocks.text: Two references are used. Absolute pressure p_abs is measured from perfect vacuum. Gauge pressure p_gauge is measured from local atmospheric pressure p_atm. The link is p_abs = p_atm + p_gauge, so p_gauge = p_abs − p_atm. A tyre gauge and a pipeline gauge usually show gauge pressure. A vacuum gives negative gauge pressure because p_abs < p_atm; the vacuum pressure is the magnitude of that negative value.

Take a vertical column of static fluid of uniform density ρ (kg/m³), cross-section A, from depth h to the free surface. Its weight is W = ρgAh, with g = 9.81 m/s². The pressure p0 at the free surface acts on the top face with force p0A, and the surrounding fluid at depth h pushes up with force pA. Equilibrium gives pA = p0A + ρgAh. Divide by A: p = p0 + ρgh. Here p is pressure at depth h, p0 is pressure at the free surface, ρ is density, g is gravity, and h is depth measured downward.

blocks.where: p is pressure at depth h in Pa; p0 is pressure at the free surface in Pa; ρ is density in kg/m³; g is 9.81 m/s²; h is depth below the free surface in m.

blocks.text: At an open surface p0 = p_atm. Then gauge pressure is p_gauge = p − p_atm = ρgh. For water, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, so each metre adds 9.81 kPa. At 5 m, gauge pressure is 49.05 kPa. In a sealed tank p0 may differ from atmosphere; use the full p0 + ρgh.

Pressure head is pressure written as a column height of the same fluid: h = p/(ρg). It has units of metres. A pump developing 49.05 kPa in water has a pressure head of 5 m of water. Pressure head compares pressures without carrying pascals through every line.

Isobars are lines of constant pressure. In a static fluid of uniform density they are horizontal, because h is constant on a horizontal line. The free surface is the top isobar. Pressure also falls with elevation z: p2 − p1 = −ρg(z2 − z1), with z measured upward.

Some syllabi add a tank that accelerates uniformly. In horizontal acceleration a, the free surface tilts and is perpendicular to an effective gravity vector g_eff. Pressure still rises along g_eff, so replace g by g_eff in the depth rule. Here h is measured along g_eff, perpendicular to the isobars, not vertically. Only a few universities ask for the full treatment; the static case is the main exam target.

blocks.where: g_eff is effective gravity magnitude in m/s²; g is 9.81 m/s²; a is horizontal acceleration in m/s²; θ is the angle of the free surface to the horizontal.

blocks.text: Use depth h positive downward inside one continuous liquid of density ρ. Within that same liquid, h is negative only when the chosen reference level lies below the point, for example a pipe branch above the tank surface; then p = p0 + ρgh gives a pressure below p0, which is negative gauge pressure only if p0 is atmospheric. The equation applies only to that liquid. Never use the liquid density for the gas space above the free surface: there the pressure is essentially p0. In a sealed vessel p0 is the pressure at the reference level, not automatically atmosphere. Keep p_atm out of gauge calculations; add it only for absolute pressure. For pressure head, state whether p is gauge or absolute. Mixing them changes the answer by about 10.3 m of water at standard atmosphere.

items: Write the data and convert all lengths to metres and pressures to pascals.
Choose the reference: use p0 = p_atm for absolute pressure, or p0 = 0 for gauge pressure in an open tank.
Take h positive downward from the free surface.
If pressure head is asked, use h = p/(ρg) with the same pressure type.

figure.caption: Gauge pressure in water rises linearly with depth: 9.81 kPa for every metre, reaching 49.05 kPa at 5 m. The straight line passes through zero at the free surface.

spec.aria: Gauge pressure in water rises linearly with depth from 0 kPa at the surface to 49.05 kPa at 5 m.

examples.question: At a point 5 m below the free surface of a tank of water open to atmosphere, find the gauge pressure, the absolute pressure and the pressure head. Take p_atm = 101.3 kPa, ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Depth h = 5 m. The tank is open, so the pressure at the free surface is p0 = p_atm = 101.3 kPa.
Gauge pressure: p_gauge = ρgh = 1000 × 9.81 × 5 = 49,050 Pa = 49.05 kPa.
Absolute pressure: p_abs = p_atm + p_gauge = 101.3 + 49.05 = 150.35 kPa.
Gauge pressure head: h = p_gauge/(ρg) = 49,050/(1000 × 9.81) = 5 m of water.
examples.answer: Gauge pressure is 49.05 kPa, absolute pressure is 150.35 kPa, and the gauge pressure head is 5 m of water.
examples.check:
rho = 1000
g = 9.81
h = 5.0
p_gauge = rho * g * h
p_gauge_kpa = p_gauge / 1000.0
p_atm = 101.3
p_abs_kpa = p_atm + p_gauge_kpa
head = p_gauge / (rho * g)
print(p_gauge)
print(p_gauge_kpa)
print(p_abs_kpa)
print(head)

traps: Adding atmospheric pressure when the question asks for gauge pressure; in an open tank the p_atm term cancels.
Measuring h upward from the bottom; h is depth downward from the free surface.
Setting p0 = 0 in a sealed tank; p0 is the pressure at the reference surface.
Using absolute pressure in a pressure-head calculation when gauge head is asked; state the reference.
Treating pressure as a vector or using total force instead of normal force per area.

quiz.q: Define gauge pressure and write its relation to absolute pressure.
quiz.a: Gauge pressure is pressure measured above local atmospheric pressure: p_gauge = p_abs − p_atm. It is negative when p_abs < p_atm.

quiz.q: Why are isobars horizontal in a static fluid of uniform density?
quiz.a: For a continuous body of the same fluid, with the same pressure p0 at the reference surface, every point on a horizontal line has the same depth h. Then p = p0 + ρgh is the same at every point, so pressure is constant along that line.

quiz.q: Find the gauge pressure 3 m below the free surface of water. Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
A gauge reads −20 kPa. Take p_atm = 100 kPa. Find absolute pressure and explain the negative sign.
quiz.a: p_abs = p_atm + p_gauge = 100 − 20 = 80 kPa. The negative gauge value means the pressure is 20 kPa below atmosphere, so the vacuum pressure is 20 kPa.

quiz.q: What pressure head in water corresponds to a gauge pressure of 49.05 kPa? Take ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².
Why does an open tank use p_gauge = ρgh instead of p0 + ρgh?
quiz.a: For an open tank p0 = p_atm. Subtracting p_atm from p = p_atm + ρgh leaves p_gauge = ρgh.

quiz.q: A sealed tank has air at 120 kPa absolute above water. Find the gauge pressure at 4 m depth. Take p_atm = 101.3 kPa, ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s².

beyond: Not for the exam. Hydrostatic pressure drives dam and retaining-wall design, tank thickness rules and pressure-sensor calibration. In meteorology, the same dp/dz = −ρg appears in the barometric formula, with density changing with height. In computational fluid dynamics, hydrostatic pressure is often split from the flow pressure to keep numerical errors small. Search next for hydrostatic pressure, pressure head, and effective gravity in an accelerating tank.
